t: I just installed the app. Where do I start?
b: Add your accounts first (Net Worth → New Account), then set budgets for the categories you actually watch. Everything else — goals, the planner, sharing — builds on those two. If you already track money elsewhere, use Import instead of typing it in.

t: Do I need to create an account or sign up?
b: No. There is no account, no email, no password. The app opens straight into your own data. If you want it on more than one device, turn on iCloud Sync — that uses the Apple ID you already have.

t: Can I try it without entering my real finances?
b:
Yes — Settings → Privacy & Security → Demo Mode swaps the whole app over to a full set of sample accounts, a year of transactions, budgets, goals and a plan.

Your real data is not copied, edited or moved while it is on. It simply isn't loaded, and it comes straight back when you exit.

It is useful well beyond trying the app out: it is the safe place to explore a feature you have never used, and the safe way to show somebody what the app does without your own finances on screen. Sharing works in there too — sample people, live switches, and nothing you touch reaches a real share.

t: What do the main screens do?
b: Home is today's picture. Budget is what's left to spend. Transactions is the ledger. Net Worth is everything you own and owe. Plan is the retirement planner. Everything else lives in the sidebar.

t: Where did a feature go? I can't find it.
b:
Three places, in this order:

1. SEARCH THIS HELP — nearly every answer names the exact route to a screen, so searching for the thing usually beats hunting for it.
2. THE MORE TAB — anything not on one of the main tabs lives there, grouped.
3. SETTINGS — if it is a preference rather than a screen.

On the Mac, ⌘F searches the whole app from anywhere, including screens you have never opened.

And if something really has moved and you had to hunt, tell us. That is a design problem, not a you problem.

t: I got a new phone. How do I move everything across?
b:
If iCloud Sync is on, there is nothing to do beyond signing into the same Apple Account and opening the app — your data arrives on its own. Give the first sync a minute; it is the slow one.

If sync is off, restore from a backup instead: Settings → Data & Backup → Backup on the old phone, then restore that file on the new one.

🔴 Do this BEFORE you wipe the old phone. A local database that was never synced and never backed up does not exist anywhere else — that is the same privacy promise working against you.

t: How do I start over and delete everything?
b:
Settings → Data & Backup. You can remove sample data on its own (“Remove Sample Data”) if you only want the demo figures gone, or clear the database entirely to begin from nothing.

Take a backup first if there is any chance you want it back. Deleting is immediate and there is no undo — see “I deleted something by accident”.

t: Can I change the currency?
b: Yes — Settings → Appearance, alongside the theme and accent color. It changes how every amount is displayed. It does not convert anything: entering 100 after a currency change stores 100, not a converted figure.

t: Can I choose which tab the app opens on?
b: Settings → General → opening tab. If you check the same screen every morning, make it that one.

t: Can I change the accent color or use dark mode?
b:
Settings → Appearance — theme (light, dark or follow the system), accent color and currency all live there.

Green and red always mean money in and money out, whatever accent you pick. That pair is not decoration and does not change.

t: Two screens show different totals for the same thing. Why?
b:
Four rules decide what a figure includes, and almost every mismatch is one of them rather than an error.

1. THE PERIOD. A month view and a year view of the same category are supposed to differ. Check the selector at the top of each screen before anything else.
2. THE SCOPE. With business mode on, personal figures exclude business money entirely, and business figures exclude personal. The same category can hold both.
3. SPLITS. A transaction split across categories contributes only its SHARE to each one — a $400 receipt at 25% business moves the business figure by $100, not $400.
4. TRANSFERS. Money moved between your own accounts is neither income nor spending, so paying off a card doesn't appear as a purchase.

If all four match and the figures still disagree, that is worth reporting — include both screens and both numbers.

t: Which date decides the month a transaction lands in?
b:
The date on the transaction — the one you can see and edit — not the date you entered it and not the date it cleared your bank.

This is why an imported charge can appear in last month after you import today, and it is the correct behavior: a dinner on the 31st belongs to that month's dining budget whatever day the bank got around to posting it.

If something is in the wrong month, edit its date. Everything downstream — budgets, reports, rollover, the trend chart — follows.

t: What counts as income, and what doesn't?
Why does a category say I'm over pace on the 2nd of the month?
b:
It shouldn't — pace is bill-aware.

A naive pace draws a straight line from the 1st to the 31st, which means rent leaving on the 1st reads as “600% of pace” every single month, and the reader learns to ignore the number. Instead, pace knows WHEN the money in a category is actually expected: a category whose recurring bill falls on the 1st is supposed to be near its limit on the 2nd.

So “over pace” means over what this category normally looks like at this point in the month — not over a straight line. One rule feeds the number, the tick mark on the bar and the curve, so they cannot disagree.

t: How is net worth put together, and when is it recorded?
b:
Assets minus liabilities, right now: account balances, real-estate equity (value minus what is owed on it), vehicles, other assets, and investment holdings at their latest price — less credit cards, loans and mortgages.

The trend chart is built from SNAPSHOTS — a stored figure with a date, so the past does not silently rewrite itself when today's prices move. That is why a chart point from March still says what March said.

One consequence worth knowing: a holding whose price hasn't refreshed carries its last known price into today's figure. It is stale rather than wrong, and refreshing prices is what settles it.

t: What's the difference between today's change and total return?
b:
They answer different questions and are computed from different starting points.

• TODAY'S CHANGE measures from the PREVIOUS CLOSE. Before the market opens there is no session yet, so what you see belongs to the last completed one — the row says “at close” when that is what it is showing.
• TOTAL RETURN measures from what you PAID. It needs a cost basis; without one the row says “No cost basis” rather than showing zero.

And there are two units in play. Beside the price, a figure is PER SHARE. In the POSITION figure, it is the whole holding. “+$1.29” and “+$372” can be the same fact about 286 shares.

t: How does the forecast decide my lowest point?
b:
It walks forward day by day from your liquid balance — checking and cash, not investments — subtracting each active recurring bill on the day it is due and adding recurring income on the day it arrives. The lowest point that walk reaches is the number.

So it is only as good as your recurring items. A forecast that looks suspiciously healthy usually means a bill isn't in the app; one that looks alarming usually means income isn't.

It deliberately does NOT model your variable spending as a straight line. Guessing what you will spend on dining would make the figure look precise without making it true.

t: How is “who spent what” worked out in a household?
b:
By WHO ADDED the transaction, not by whose money it was. Those are different questions and the app used to run one through the other.

Every row added since the app started recording authorship carries its author, and the feed, the split bar and the Mine / Theirs / Joint filter all read that.

Rows entered BEFORE that have no author at all, and they say “Joint”. That is honest rather than a guess — the information does not exist for those rows and inventing it would put words in somebody's mouth.

t: Why doesn't my partner's copy show the same total as mine?
b:
Three legitimate reasons before it is a fault:

1. KEPT PRIVATE. Anything either of you held back is not in the other's figures — it was never sent, so it cannot be counted.
2. FRESHNESS. A summary is published by the sender's device while the app is open. If they haven't opened it since yesterday, yesterday is the newest figure that exists anywhere.
3. WHEN YOU JOINED. Years tracked before you shared are yours unless you chose to bring the history across, and that choice is deliberately opt-in.

In a full-access household with nothing kept private and both apps recently open, the totals should match. If they don't, that one is worth sending in.

t: Why does spending on my credit card make the balance go UP?
b:
Because a credit-card balance is what you OWE, not what you have.

A $150 charge increases what you owe, so the balance rises and your net worth falls by $150. Paying the card is a transfer: money leaves checking, the card balance falls, and your net worth doesn't move at all — you swapped cash for a smaller debt.

That last part is why a card payment is not spending. The spending already happened on the day of the charge, and counting the payment too would count it twice.

t: How should I record paying my credit card?
b:
As a transfer between the two accounts, not as an expense.

The purchases on the card are already in your budget, dated when you made them. If the payment were an expense as well, a $600 card payment would show up as $600 of spending on top of the $600 of purchases it settles.

This is the single most common way a budget total ends up looking twice as bad as the month really was.

t: Is my financial data private?
b:
Yes, and it is worth being specific about what that means rather than just asserting it.

Your finances live in a database on your device. If you turn on iCloud Sync, a copy also lives in YOUR private iCloud — the same place your photos and messages go, reachable only by your Apple ID. We have no server holding any of it, so there is nothing on our side to breach, subpoena or sell.

The app makes exactly one kind of outbound request: market prices for the tickers you hold or watch. That request carries a symbol like AAPL and nothing else — no balances, no holdings, no identity.

There is no analytics SDK, no advertising SDK and no crash reporter phoning home.

t: Do you sell or share my data?
b:
Never, and the architecture is what makes that true rather than a promise.

There is no advertising SDK in the app, no analytics broker, and no server of ours that holds your finances — there is nowhere for it to be sold FROM. Your data is on your device and, if you turn sync on, in your own private iCloud, which we cannot read.

What we do see: nothing, unless you send it. If you use Report a Problem and leave “Attach device info” on, we get the app version, the iOS version, and counts — how many accounts, how many transactions. The exact text is shown to you in full before it sends; “includes some technical info” is how an app that respects privacy still ends up feeling like one that doesn't.

The business model is the app itself, not you.

t: Where exactly is my data stored?
b:
In a database file inside the app's own storage on your device, and nowhere else until you choose otherwise.

Turn on iCloud Sync and a mirror also lives in YOUR private iCloud — the same place your photo library and device backups live, under your Apple Account, encrypted in transit and at rest. We have no access to it and no copy of it.

Turn on iCloud Drive backups and a backup file is written to a folder you can open in the Files app. That one you can see, move and delete yourself.

Any report or CSV you export goes wherever you send it, and at that point it is an ordinary file with ordinary file rules.

t: What is Demo Mode?
b:
It swaps the whole app over to realistic sample data — a full set of accounts, a year of transactions, budgets and a plan — so you can explore every screen, or show someone what the app does, without your own finances on display.

Your real data is not copied, edited or moved while Demo Mode is on. It simply isn't loaded, and it comes straight back when you exit.

It is genuinely useful for more than demos: it is the safe place to try a feature you haven't used before.

t: Is Simple Finance free?
b:
Right now, yes — free, and no ads. Everything you see is included: budgeting, net worth, the retirement planner, sharing, all of it.

If you are using it today, it stays free for you. That is not a trial and it does not quietly expire — early users are grandfathered in.

At some point new users will pay a subscription instead. That applies to people who have not downloaded it yet, not to you.

t: How do I sync between my iPhone and Mac?
b:
Sign both devices into the same Apple ID, then turn on iCloud Sync in Settings on EACH one — it is off until you turn it on, and it takes effect after the app restarts.

Accounts, transactions, budgets, goals, investments and your plan all mirror through your own private iCloud. The first sync after switching it on is the slow one; after that changes usually land within seconds of the other device opening the app.

One thing that surprises people: nothing syncs to an app that isn't running. A device you haven't opened in a week shows last week's numbers until you open it.

t: How do I back up my data?
b:
Two ways, and they do different jobs.

A JSON backup (Settings → Data & Backup) writes everything to a single file you own and can put anywhere — it is your escape hatch, and the thing to take before any big change. There is also a weekly automatic backup to your iCloud Drive if you turn it on.

iCloud Sync is NOT a backup. It mirrors your current state, so deleting something on one device deletes it everywhere. That is what sync is for; it is not what protects you from a mistake.

Restores are additive — they add what's missing rather than wiping what's there — so restoring an old file will never empty your app.

t: Will I lose data if I delete the app?
b: Your iCloud-synced copy and any JSON/iCloud-Drive backups survive a delete. Reinstall, sign into the same Apple ID, and your data flows back. Keep a JSON backup before big changes just in case.

t: How do I restore from a backup?
b:
Settings → Data & Backup → restore, then pick the file.

Afterwards, run Settings → Data & Backup → Repair Duplicated Records. A restore on top of existing data is the single most common way to end up with the same record twice, and that screen is built for exactly this.

t: Does it back up on its own?
b:
It can — automatic backups to your own iCloud Drive, on a schedule, in a folder you can open in the Files app.

That is a different thing from iCloud Sync. Sync keeps your devices matching; a backup is a file you can restore from if something goes wrong on all of them at once. Having sync on is not a reason to skip backups.

t: How are budgets and spending calculated?
b:
Spending is summed from your own transactions, by category, for the period on screen — nothing is estimated or modeled.

A few rules decide what counts. A SPLIT transaction contributes only its share to each category. A TRANSFER between your own accounts is neither income nor spending, so paying a card off doesn't look like a purchase. If business mode is on, business money is excluded from personal figures entirely.

Your limit can be monthly or yearly, and a single month can be overridden — a bigger December — without touching the default that returns in January.

t: Can one month have a different budget than usual?
b:
Yes — open the category and set a limit for that month specifically. December's gift budget can be four times November's, and January returns to the default on its own.

The override belongs to that one month. It does not change the category's normal limit, it is not a permanent edit you have to remember to undo, and the reports know which figure applied when.

For something that is not really a month at all — a wedding, a car, a new roof — use a one-time expense instead. It sits in the annual plan and stays out of every monthly budget, so one big purchase doesn't make twelve months look broken.

t: What does Safe-to-Spend mean?
b:
It is the answer to "can I spend this?" rather than "what have I spent?"

It starts from what you actually have available, subtracts the bills still to come before your next income, subtracts what your budgets have already committed, and keeps back any reserve you asked for. What's left is the number.

It moves as the month goes on, which is the point — a figure that only updated once a month would tell you nothing on the 20th. Adding your recurring bills is what makes it accurate; without them it can't know what's coming.

t: How are my subscriptions detected?
b: The Subscriptions tab scans your transaction history for charges from the same merchant that repeat on a regular rhythm, infers the cadence, predicts the next charge, and flags price increases — all on your device. Click Track to turn any into a recurring bill.

t: What's the difference between rings and bars?
b: Only the drawing. Rings show each category as a dial, bars as a horizontal meter — same numbers, same limits. Switch with the toggle above the categories and pick whichever you read faster.

t: What is rollover?
b: Turn it on for a category and whatever you didn't spend this month is added to next month's allowance. Overspend carries the other way, and a carried overspend can never push the allowance below zero.

t: I went over on one category. Can I cover it from another?
b: Yes — that's the Cover button on an over-budget category. Pick where the money comes from and the app moves the allowance across for that month only. Your defaults are unchanged.

t: How do I budget for a wedding, a ring, or a car?
b: Add it as a one-time expense rather than a monthly category. It sits in the annual plan and deliberately stays out of every monthly budget, so a single big purchase doesn't make twelve months look broken.

t: Can I budget yearly instead of monthly?
b: Yes. A category can carry a yearly limit instead of a monthly one — useful for things like insurance or gifts that don't arrive evenly. The Budget screen switches between the monthly and annual view.

t: What are subcategories for?
b: Splitting one budget into named parts — "Personal Care" into "Therapy" and "Prescriptions", for example. They roll up into the parent's limit, so the budget still reads as one number.

t: How does the Cash Flow Forecast work?
b: It projects your liquid balance (checking + cash) forward 30–90 days using your active recurring bills and income, then shows the lowest point it'll hit and how much you can safely spend today without dipping below your buffer. Add recurring items in Transactions ▸ Recurring to make it accurate.

t: How do I add, rename or delete a category?
b:
All of it happens on the Budget tab.

• ADD — “Add Category” at the bottom of the list. Give it a name, a color and a monthly limit; the limit can be zero if you only want to track it.
• RENAME or RECOLOUR — open the category, then edit it. The change follows every transaction already filed under it; nothing is re-categorized and no history moves.
• DELETE — “Delete Category” on that same screen.

The starters that come with a fresh app are only starters. Rename, recolour or delete them until the list matches how you actually think about money — that is the single biggest thing you can do to make budgeting stick.

t: What happens to my transactions if I delete a category?
b:
They are not deleted. A transaction whose category has gone becomes uncategorised, and it keeps its date, amount, account and merchant — it simply stops counting toward any budget line.

You can re-file them in bulk: on the Transactions tab, select the rows and use “Categorize selected”.

If what you actually want is to fold one category into another rather than lose the grouping, merge them instead — see “We ended up with the same category twice”.

t: We ended up with the same category twice. How do I merge them?
b:
Settings → Data & Backup → Repair Duplicated Records → “Categories under the same name”.

Merging picks a keeper (the one carrying the most transactions) and repoints everything at it — transactions, recurring items, dated overrides, rules and coverages all follow. Subcategories are folded too, including the duplicate pair the merge itself would otherwise create.

One thing it deliberately does NOT do is add the two budgets together. Two people who both tracked $1,900 of rent do not have $3,800 of rent. You are asked which figure to keep.

This is also the screen for duplicate accounts, duplicate rows left over from a restore, and copies pulled down from an older iCloud database.

t: What are subcategories, and when should I bother?
b:
A subcategory splits one budget line into named parts without splitting the budget itself — Groceries into “Weekly shop” and “Costco runs”, Car into “Fuel”, “Insurance” and “Repairs”.

The parent keeps one limit and one ring. The subcategories tell you where inside it the money went, which is what you actually need when a category is over and you cannot see why.

Use them when a single category is big enough that “over by $180” doesn't tell you anything actionable. Skip them everywhere else — a budget with forty lines gets abandoned.

t: Can I reorder my categories?
b: Yes — the Budget tab list can be rearranged, and the order carries to the Home screen and to the reports. Put the four or five you actually watch at the top; the ones you only glance at monthly can live below the fold.

t: What does the ring on Bills & Subscriptions mean?
b: It's this month's bills: what you've logged as paid, and what's still left. The middle shows how many of them are done. It fills as bills are logged, and closes when the month is finished.

t: Why does the ring say nothing is paid?
b: The app can only count a bill as paid once there's a transaction for it. If you don't log bills, it has nothing to point at. Turn on Auto-Post Recurring and they post themselves on their due day, or log one yourself: right-click a bill in Recurring and choose Log Now.

t: What is Auto-Post Recurring?
b: With it on, each recurring bill or paycheque creates its transaction automatically on its due day, so your ledger stays current without you typing. With it off, nothing posts until you log it yourself — right-click the bill and choose Log Now.

t: Will a recurring bill ever post twice?
How do I stop a bill without deleting its history?
b:
Set it to inactive rather than deleting it. It stops posting and stops reminding, and every payment it has already made stays exactly where it is — in your spending, in the reports, in the category totals.

Deleting is a different thing: it removes the recurring RULE, and what happens to the payments already recorded depends on what you choose at the time. There is no undo afterwards.

If a subscription might come back, inactive is almost always the right answer. Reactivating is one click and the history is unbroken.

t: Can I get reminded before a bill is due?
b:
Yes. Settings → Notifications turns bill reminders on and sets how many days ahead they arrive, and an individual bill can carry its own lead time — rent three days out and a streaming charge on the day is a perfectly sensible setup.

A reminder is tied to the bill's due date, so changing the date moves the reminder with it. Marking a bill paid early cancels that month's reminder rather than firing it anyway.

t: How do I split one transaction across categories?
b: Open the transaction and use Split. A grocery run can be part Groceries and part Household, and each part counts toward its own budget — the totals still add up to what you actually paid.

t: Can I scan a receipt?
b: Yes. Add a transaction and scan the receipt — the amount and merchant are read on your device, and you confirm before anything is saved. The image can be kept with the transaction.

t: What are Rules?
b:
Rules categorize transactions for you: match a merchant, and every future transaction from them lands in the category you chose. They run on your device as transactions arrive or import.

A new rule can catch up, too: “Apply to Uncategorized” runs every enabled rule over transactions that have no category yet — which is what you want straight after an import. It deliberately leaves anything you have already filed alone, because a rule should never overwrite a decision you made by hand.

t: How do I record moving money between my own accounts?
b: Mark it as a transfer. Transfers move the balance between accounts without counting as income or spending, so paying off a card or moving to savings doesn't distort your budget.

t: How do I find an old transaction?
b:
The Transactions tab has search and filters — text, category, account, amount range, date range, and in a household whether it was yours, theirs or joint. They stack, so “groceries over $100 last autumn” is three filters rather than a long scroll.

On the Mac, ⌘F searches everything from anywhere in the app.

If you cannot remember the merchant, search the AMOUNT instead. People remember what a thing cost far more reliably than what the card statement called the shop.

t: I deleted something by accident. Can I undo it?
b: There's no undo, so a delete is final — that's why anything destructive asks first. Keep a JSON backup (Settings → Data & Backup) before a big clear-out, and a restore will bring the rows back.

t: How do I split a bill with other people?
b:
Turn on “Split this bill” on the transaction and say how many people are in on it.

🔴 Enter the FULL total, not your share. The app records your share and keeps the whole figure for context — which is what you want when the receipt says $120 and your budget should only feel $40.

t: Can I edit or categorize a lot of transactions at once?
b:
Yes. On the Transactions tab, select the rows and use “Categorize selected”. This is the fast way to clean up after an import, or after deleting a category.

If the same fix keeps coming up, make it a Rule instead and it happens on its own from then on.

t: How do I mark something as reimbursable?
b:
Mark it on the transaction. It stays in your spending — it really did leave your account — but it is flagged so you can see what is owed back, and on the business side it can be billed on to a client as an invoice line.

Reimbursable is a claim you make deliberately. Nothing sets it for you.

t: How do I find and remove duplicate transactions?
b:
Settings → Data & Backup → Repair Duplicated Records. It scans for the same record present as several rows — which is what a re-import or a restore produces — and shows you what it found before removing anything.

It is deliberately conservative. Two coffees on the same day at the same shop are two coffees; it is looking for the same RECORD twice, not two similar ones.

t: How do I add accounts?
b:
Net Worth tab → + → Add Account. Pick the type — checking, savings, credit card, loan, mortgage, brokerage, retirement, cash, vehicle, real estate or a catch-all other asset — and give it a starting balance.

The type is not cosmetic. It decides whether the balance counts as an asset or a debt, whether the account can hold investments, and how it is treated in reports.

Two behaviors worth knowing at the start:
• TRACKED accounts compute their balance from a starting figure plus the transactions since. Enter transactions and the balance keeps itself.
• MANUAL accounts hold whatever you type. Nothing updates them for you; you set the balance when you check it.

Give an account its own icon and color once you have more than a handful — you stop reading a list of similar names and start recognizing a shape.

t: Are account balances updated automatically?
b: Investment holdings revalue from live prices. Manual accounts (checking, cash, property) hold the balance you enter — the Accounts view flags any that have gone stale so they're easy to refresh.

t: How is net worth calculated?
b: Total assets minus total liabilities, including real-estate equity and investment holdings. The trend chart snapshots it over time so you can see the direction, not just today's number.

t: Can I track my house and car?
b: Yes. Real estate, vehicles and other property are account types, and a mortgage or auto loan can be linked so that each payment moves principal off the balance instead of just leaving the debt sitting there.

t: What are net-worth snapshots?
b: A record of what you were worth on a date, so the trend line has real history rather than being recalculated from today's balances. They're taken as you use the app and can be shared with a household.

t: Can I give an account its own icon and color?
b: Yes — open the account and pick one. It is worth doing once you have more than a handful: on the Net Worth tab and in every picker afterwards, you are looking for a shape and a color rather than reading a list of similar names.

t: Why did my net worth change when I renamed an investment account?
b:
It shouldn't, and if it did, the holdings lost their link to the account. Open the account and check the holdings are still listed under it.

This was a real defect and it is fixed — but a database that went through it once may still be carrying the orphans. If the holdings are gone from the account but still in your portfolio, re-link them there.

t: My balance here doesn't match my bank. How do I fix it?
b:
Open Net Worth and click Reconcile in the toolbar. It puts every account in one sheet so you can sit down with your bank tabs open and make the whole picture true in one pass.

Type what each account really says today. Blank rows are left alone, so doing the three that matter and ignoring the rest is a perfectly good way to use it.

The difference is recorded as a balance adjustment rather than by rewriting anything — every transaction you have already entered stays exactly as it was.

t: Does reconciling change my transaction history?
b:
No. It adds one dated balance adjustment for the difference and leaves everything else alone.

That is deliberate: your history is what actually happened, and an app that quietly edited old rows to make a total come out right would be destroying the only record you have. The adjustment is visible, and you can see exactly when and how much.

t: How often should I reconcile?
b:
Once a month is plenty, and it is essentially the whole maintenance routine for an app that isn't linked to a bank.

Reconcile All also records a net-worth snapshot as it applies, which is what puts a point on your trajectory chart — so the habit that keeps your balances honest is the same one that makes the projection worth reading.

t: Where do stock and crypto prices come from?
b: Public market data, fetched only for the tickers you hold or watch. It's the one thing the app sends to the internet, and it sends a symbol — never your holdings, balances or identity.

t: Can I track cost basis and tax lots?
b:
Yes. A holding can carry individual lots — shares, price paid and date — rather than one blended average, which is what you need when only part of a position is sold.

Cost basis is optional. Without it a holding still tracks its value; you just don't see gain or loss, and the row says “No cost basis” rather than “$0.00”, because those are very different claims.

With lots recorded, the Tax Preparation Pack can show what a sale looks like against them.

t: Can I compare my portfolio to the market?
b:
Yes — chart your holdings against an index over the same period and read the two lines together.

One thing to read carefully: the portfolio line prices your CURRENT shares at past prices. It is what you hold today, valued backwards through time — not a record of the trades you actually made. That makes it the right tool for “how has this basket done” and the wrong one for “how have I done”, which depends on when you bought.

t: Why doesn't my mutual fund move during the day?
b: Because mutual funds don't have an intraday price. They're valued once, after the close, so a fund's number legitimately sits still while stocks move — it isn't a stale reading.

t: Can I invest a set amount every month automatically?
b:
You can plan it. Set up an auto-invest plan with the amount, the schedule and the holdings, and the app tracks the contributions and what they bought against your plan.

It does not move real money or place a trade — no app that keeps your data on your own device can. It is the record and the projection, and you make the transfer at your brokerage.

t: Can I track crypto?
b: Yes — coins are held and priced alongside your stocks and funds, and they count into net worth the same way. Prices come from a public market source; history on the free tier goes back a year.

t: What's the difference between the dollar figures on a holding row?
b:
There are two, and they are not the same fact:

• Beside the PRICE, per share — what one share moved today. “+$1.29” means the price went from $348.96 to $350.25.
• In the POSITION figure, for the whole holding — what your holding moved. On 286 shares, that same move is “+$372”.

Use the column header to switch it between market value, today's change and total return.

t: How do investments reconcile?
b:
By SHARE COUNT, not by value — you type how many shares you really hold, not what the position is worth.

A correction is added at your average cost, so your return does not move when you fix a share count. Reconciling on value instead would silently rewrite your gain or loss, which is the number most people are actually watching.

t: How do I set a savings goal?
b:
Goals → “Add a goal”. There are four kinds and they answer different questions:

• SAVE UP — a target amount by a target date (a trip, a deposit, a new roof). It tells you the monthly figure that gets you there and flags the goal “At risk” if the pace stops working.
• PAY DOWN — the same thing pointed at a debt, tracking what you have paid off rather than what you have put aside.
• NET WORTH — a whole-picture target rather than one pot.
• RETIREMENT — hands off to the planner, because that one is a projection and not a straight line.

An Emergency Fund goal is a Save Up goal with a shortcut: set a monthly figure and it sizes the fund for you.

t: How does a goal know how much I've saved?
b:
Link it to the account holding the money, and progress is that account's real balance — nothing to update by hand, and it moves the moment the balance does.

If you would rather not link one, you can enter progress yourself, but then the goal only knows what you have told it. A goal that never moves is almost always an unlinked one.

t: What does “At risk” on a goal mean?
b:
The current pace does not reach the target by the date. It is arithmetic, not a judgment: what is left, divided by the months remaining, against what you have actually been putting in.

Three things fix it and the app does not choose for you — move the date, lower the target, or raise the monthly amount.

t: Can a goal have a picture?
b: Yes, and it is worth doing. A goal with a photo of the actual thing gets funded more often than one called “House Fund”. Add it when you create the goal or from the goal's own screen.

t: How accurate is the retirement planner?
b: It runs a month-by-month simulation of your accounts, income, taxes, and spending, then stress-tests it against 500 random market futures and every real market since 1928. It's a rigorous estimate — not a guarantee — and clearly labeled as such.

t: What do the Monte Carlo results mean?
b: The success rate is the share of simulated market futures in which your money outlasts your plan. 90% means the plan survived 9 of 10 random histories. Use it to compare choices, not as a promise.

t: What is the Financial Health Score?
b:
A single 0–100 score built from FIVE pillars — emergency fund, savings rate, debt load, net worth and budget adherence — each with a plain-English recommendation and a link to the screen that improves it.

Retirement pace is a sixth pillar that is not scored yet: it needs a birthday and an income to compare against, which you set in Settings → Profile. The screen says so where the score is shown.

The pillars are weighted by impact, so the fastest way up is whichever one is lowest. Everything is computed on your device from data already in the app.

t: Can Fin answer questions about my forecast and subscriptions?
b: Yes. Fin is grounded in your live data, so you can ask things like "will I make it to payday?", "how much can I safely spend?", "what are my subscriptions?", "did any go up?", "how am I doing?", and "am I balanced?" — and it answers from your forecast, detected subscriptions, health score, and allocation.

t: What's on the Tools tab?
b:
Sixteen calculators, your saved calculations, and the Tax Center.

They are grouped by what you are trying to do rather than by name:
• KILL DEBT — Debt Payoff, Credit Card, Student Loan, Biweekly Payoff, Refinance.
• BUY A HOME — Mortgage / Loan, Home Affordability, Rent vs. Buy, Auto Loan.
• SAVE & INVEST — Compound Interest, Savings Goal, Emergency Fund, FIRE / Retire Early, Retirement, Roth vs. Traditional.
• INCOME & SPENDING — Take-Home Pay, Subscriptions, Tax Estimator.

None of them touch your real data. They are scratch paper with good arithmetic.

t: Which calculator should I use?
b:
The short map:

• “Should I overpay the mortgage or invest it?” — Mortgage / Loan, then Compound Interest.
• “Which debt first?” — Debt Payoff. It compares avalanche (highest rate) against snowball (smallest balance) on your actual numbers.
• “Is refinancing worth it?” — Refinance. The answer is a break-even month, not a yes.
• “What will I actually take home?” — Take-Home Pay.
• “Can I afford this house?” — Home Affordability, then Rent vs. Buy for the second half of the question.
• “How big should my emergency fund be?” — Emergency Fund.
• “Roth or Traditional?” — Roth vs. Traditional, which turns on the tax rate you expect later, not the one you pay now.
• “When could I stop working?” — FIRE / Retire Early for the quick version, the Retirement Planner for the honest one.

t: Can I save a calculation and come back to it?
b:
Yes — “Save This Calculation”, give it a name, and it lands in Saved Calculations on the Tools tab. Every input is kept, so you can reopen it months later and change one number instead of rebuilding the whole thing.

This is what makes the calculators useful for a decision you are sitting on rather than one you make once. Save “Refinance at 5.75%” today and the comparison is still there when the rate moves.

t: Do the calculators change my real budget or accounts?
b: No. Nothing on the Tools tab writes to your data. You can put any number in any field without consequence — that is the point of having them separate from the tabs that do.

t: What does the Tax Estimator do?
b:
It gives you a rough federal picture from income, filing status and the deductions you enter — enough to answer “am I going to owe?” before it is too late to do anything about it.

It is an estimate and it is not tax advice. It does not know about every credit, state tax, or anything unusual in your situation. If it says you are close to a line that matters, that is the signal to talk to someone who files for a living.

t: What's in the Tax Center?
b:
The year's tax-relevant figures pulled together: deductible categories, rental Schedule-E export, and — if the business side is switched on — the Schedule C summary, mileage at the rate you set, and reimbursable costs.

It is a starting pack for whoever prepares your return, not a filing tool.

t: How do I export a PDF report?
b:
Settings → Data & Backup → Reports. Pick one, preview it, then export or share.

The set:
• COMPLETE FINANCIAL REPORT — everything, in order.
• NET WORTH STATEMENT — assets, debts and the number, as of a date.
• INCOME & SPENDING — where it came from and where it went.
• BUDGET PERFORMANCE — plan against actual, category by category.
• INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO — holdings, allocation, cost basis and return.
• BUDGET TO SHARE — the one built to hand to somebody else.
• RETIREMENT READINESS — the plan's own summary.
• TAX PREPARATION PACK — the year's figures for whoever files.
• DEBT & PAYOFF — balances, rates and the payoff order.
• SUBSCRIPTION AUDIT — every recurring charge, what it costs a year, and what has gone up.

t: How do I send someone my numbers without showing my net worth?
b:
Two ways, and they solve different halves of it.

• “Budget to Share” is a report built for this — spending and plan, no balances and no net worth.
• Any other report has a “Hide everything that shows balances” button. Use it. The cover page of a Complete Financial Report prints your net worth in large type otherwise, which is a surprise nobody wants at the accountant's desk.

If what you want is an ongoing view rather than a document, share a summary instead — you tick exactly what it includes and anything switched off is never sent.

t: Can I export to a spreadsheet or CSV?
b:
Yes — transactions export as CSV, which opens in Numbers, Excel or Google Sheets.

One deliberate detail: any field starting with =, +, - or @ is written so a spreadsheet treats it as text rather than a formula. A merchant called “=SUM” is a merchant name, not something your spreadsheet should run.

t: Can I print?
b:
On the Mac, ⌘P prints whatever is on screen, and every report can be printed from its preview.

On iPhone and iPad, export the report and print from the share sheet.

t: Can I export a single account's statement?
b: Yes — open the account and export an Account Statement for a date range. It is the right thing to hand over when somebody wants one account rather than your whole financial life.

t: What can the app notify me about?
b:
Settings → Notifications, and every one of them is individually switchable:

• BILL REMINDERS — before something is due, at the lead time you choose.
• BUDGET ALERTS — when a category is close to its limit, or over it.
• LOW BALANCE — when the forecast says an account is heading below your buffer.
• LARGE TRANSACTION — anything over an amount you set.
• WEEKLY AND MONTHLY REVIEW — a short summary of what happened.
• SMART INSIGHTS — a subscription that went up, spending well off its usual pattern, a bill that didn't arrive.

Nothing is on by default that you have not agreed to, and turning the whole lot off does not affect anything else in the app.

t: I'm getting too many notifications.
b:
Settings → Notifications and turn off the categories you do not act on. The usual culprits are budget alerts on categories with small limits, and large-transaction alerts set too low.

If they arrive in a clump rather than being individually wrong, that is the thing to change — one review a week tells you more than nine alerts a day, because nine alerts a day become wallpaper.

t: What is the Weekly or Monthly Review?
b:
A short read-through of what actually happened: what you spent against plan, what moved most, what is coming up, and anything that looks unlike your normal month.

It is the one notification worth leaving on if you turn everything else off, because it is the only one that asks for a couple of minutes rather than a reaction.

t: Can I share finances with a partner or family?
b:
Yes, in three different shapes depending on who it is.

A PARTNER shares fully and both ways: you both see and edit the same accounts, transactions, budgets and goals, and every shared transaction records who added it.

FAMILY gets a read-only summary you control — net worth, income, goals, bills, trends, or only the categories you choose.

FRIENDS see only the specific numbers you put in a scorecard, and nothing else.

All three run through your own iCloud, so nothing passes through us. Open the sidebar → Family & Sharing to start. Anything you keep private is removed from their device on the next sync rather than simply going stale, and business money is never shared at all.

t: What's the difference between sharing with a partner, family and friends?
b: A partner gets full two-way access: you both see and edit the same accounts, transactions, budgets and goals. Family gets a read-only summary you control. Friends see only the specific numbers you choose to put in a scorecard. They're separate, and joining one doesn't join you to the others.

t: How do I start sharing with my partner?
b: Open the sidebar → Family & Sharing, and send an invitation. They accept on their device and the two of you are joined through your own iCloud — there is no account on our side and nothing passes through our servers.

t: Can I keep some things private from my partner?
b: Yes. Any category, account, bill, investment account, mortgage, retirement plan, goal or single transaction can be kept private. Making something private also removes the copy already on their device on the next sync — it doesn't merely stop updating it.

t: Does my partner see the years I tracked before we shared?
b: Only if you hand it over. Your earlier history stays yours by default, and there's a switch to share it — useful when one of you is new to the app and the other has years of it. A month they already have is never counted twice.

t: How do we combine two sets of finances?
b: Combine Finances walks it once: choose which accounts belong to the household, and for any category you both tracked, choose which budget to keep. It's a single pass rather than a merge that guesses.

t: Can we see who spent what?
b: Yes. Every shared transaction shows who added it, and the month's spending splits into a column for each of you plus one for shared household spending — rather than one lump you have to untangle.

t: Which categories count as household?
b: Rent, utilities, groceries, insurance and the like start out as shared, because they usually are. Everything else starts personal, and any category or single transaction can be changed at any time.

t: Can we tell each other apart at a glance?
b: Yes — each of you gets a color and a picture, and they follow you onto every screen: the split bar, the activity feed and the notes board. Colors and pictures are set on your own device.

t: What happens if we stop sharing?
b: The shared copy is removed from their device. Anything you entered stays yours, and anything they entered stays theirs — neither of you is left holding half of the other's ledger.

t: Is business money shared with my household?
b:
No, and it is enforced rather than assumed. Business transactions, business accounts and business clients are excluded from everything a household partner receives — not sent and then hidden, never sent.

That holds the other way too: a partner's household view cannot reveal what a client paid you or what a job cost.

If something is genuinely both — a phone bill that is half work — split it by percentage. Only the personal share reaches the household side, and only the business share reaches the Schedule C figure.

t: I imported my bank transactions but my account balance didn't change
b:
Two things have to be true, and each one is easy to miss because the app does something reasonable without them.

1. THE TRANSACTIONS MUST BE ASSIGNED TO THE ACCOUNT. On the import screen there is an “Import into” picker. It now starts on your default account, but if it is set to “No account” the rows still import — they just belong to no account, so no balance can follow them. Fix an import you already did from Transactions: select the rows and set the account.

2. THE ACCOUNT MUST TRACK ITS BALANCE. Open the account and check “Track balance from transactions”. New checking, savings and cash accounts turn this on for you. When it is OFF the balance is a number you type and nothing changes it — which is right for a house or a car, and wrong for a current account.

With both on, the balance is your starting balance as of the tracking date, plus every assigned transaction after it. That figure is what Net Worth shows.

One thing that is NOT a fault: your opening balance does not appear in Year in Review or in spending totals. It is a starting position, not income — money you already had rather than money that came in.

t: How do I import existing accounts or transactions?
b: The Import tab reads accounts and loans from a photo or CSV and auto-classifies them for review before anything is saved. You approve the results — nothing imports silently.

t: What files can I import?
b:
CSV and TSV from almost any bank or app, OFX and QFX from a bank download, Excel workbooks (.xlsx), and a photo or PDF of a statement read by OCR.

The file does not have to be tidy. Columns are matched by what is IN them rather than by their headings, so a file whose date column is called “Posted” and whose amount column is called “Debit” works without renaming anything. Dates in almost any order, amounts in parentheses, a trailing minus, currency symbols and thousands separators are all understood.

Apple Numbers' own .numbers format is not supported — export it as CSV or Excel first, which Numbers does in two clicks.

Everything is review-first. You see every row, and nothing is written until you say so.

t: My import shows odd characters like “café”. Why?
b: That's a file saved in an older text encoding. The app tries the common ones in order and should read it correctly — if a file still looks wrong, send it to us through Report a Problem and we'll fix the reader.

t: Will importing create duplicates?
b:
It works hard not to. Rows matching something already in your ledger — same date, same amount, same account — are flagged during the review step, and you decide whether they are one charge or two identical ones.

Two $4.50 coffees on the same day at the same shop is a real thing that happens, which is why it asks rather than silently dropping the second.

If duplicates do get through — usually from importing the same file twice, or restoring a backup on top of live data — Settings → Data & Backup → Repair Duplicated Records finds them and shows you what it found before removing anything.

t: Does it work on iPad, Mac and Apple Watch?
b:
Yes, all three, and they are real apps rather than a phone screen stretched.

• IPAD — opens in a tab layout with a sidebar available, and the wider screens lay out in two columns.
• MAC — a proper Mac app: sidebar, ⌘F search, ⌘P printing, ⌘N for a new entry, and Budget or the Retirement Planner can each open in their own window beside the main one. It is the same purchase, not a separate one to buy.
• APPLE WATCH — today's spending against pace, what is left in the budget, net worth, and your holdings merged by ticker with a sparkline and today's move. Complications put one figure on the watch face itself.

Widgets cover the home screen, the lock screen and StandBy, and quick-log writes a purchase straight from a widget without opening the app.

t: What can the widgets show?
b: Desktop and Notification Center widgets for what's left to spend, cash flow and net worth, plus a watch complication. There's also a quick-log widget for adding a transaction without opening the app.

t: Can I lock the app?
b: Yes — Touch ID or your Apple Watch on open, in Settings → Privacy & Security. There's also Hide Amounts to blur every figure on screen, which is the one to use when someone's looking over your shoulder.

t: What does the Apple Watch app show?
b:
The short answers, on the wrist: today's spending against pace, what is left in the budget, your net worth, and your holdings — merged by ticker, with a sparkline and today's move rather than yesterday's total.

Complications put the number you care about on the watch face itself, and the rectangular one is designed to be legible on the smallest 40mm watch rather than on an Ultra.

t: Can I log a purchase from a widget?
b: Yes — quick-log writes straight from the widget without opening the app, and it can be undone from the widget too if you fat-finger it. The undo touches only that entry.

t: I placed a widget and now I want it to show something else.
b:
Right-click the widget → Edit Widget, and pick the metric there.

🔴 The choice belongs to that PLACED widget, not to the app. Changing the default in the app does not reach a widget already placed on your desktop or in Notification Center — you either edit that widget or remove and re-add it.

t: Is business money mixed in with my personal budget?
b: No. Business and personal are separate throughout, with one switch to change which you're looking at. A transaction can be split between them by percentage when something is genuinely both.

t: What does the business side include?
b:
Enough to run a small trade or a side business without a second app:

• CLIENTS AND JOBS — who you work for, what you are working on, and what each job made.
• ESTIMATES AND INVOICES — built from a price list, sent as a PDF, tracked through to paid, with a month-end run that invoices everything outstanding in one pass.
• A WORK TIMER AND WORK LOG — hours against a job, which become an invoice line or a cost.
• MILEAGE — logged per business and deducted at the rate you set.
• EXPENSES — deductible by default, attributable to a client, and markable reimbursable so they can be billed on.
• CREW — employee hours, an approvals queue, and per-person seats with roles.
• RECEIVABLES — what is owed and how late it is.
• A SCHEDULE C SUMMARY at tax time, with the home-office cap and a set-aside figure.

It is off until you turn it on, and it stays completely out of the way when you don't.

t: How do I turn the business side on — and off again?
b:
Settings → Business. Add a business, and a switch appears for moving between Personal and Business.

Until you do that, none of it exists: no extra tabs, no business rows in your ledger, nothing added to any screen. Turning it off later hides it again — it does not delete anything you entered, and a business you archive keeps its history rather than losing it.

You can run more than one business, and they do not see each other's money.

t: How do I invoice a customer?
b:
Build the invoice from your price list, or from the hours and costs already logged against the job — that is the point of logging them there.

• An ESTIMATE can become an invoice without retyping it.
• A work-log entry becomes a line, at the rate you set.
• A cost marked REIMBURSABLE can be billed on as its own line.

Send it as a PDF and track it through to paid. Receivables shows what is outstanding and how late it is, and the month-end run invoices everything outstanding in one pass rather than one customer at a time.

t: Can employees log their own hours?
b:
Yes. Each crew member gets their own seat with a role, logs hours against jobs from their own device, and what they submit lands in an approvals queue rather than straight into your books. You approve it, and only then does it become cost and invoice lines.

A seat sees its own work. One employee cannot see another's hours, your customers' details or your money.

t: How does mileage and the Schedule C summary work?
b:
Log a trip against a business and it is deducted at the rate YOU set — the rate is not baked in, because it changes and because your situation may differ.

The Schedule C summary pulls the year together: gross receipts (money in only), expenses by line, mileage, the home-office cap, net profit, and a set-aside figure so a profitable year doesn't arrive as a surprise in April. A loss sets aside nothing rather than a negative number.

It is a preparation pack, not a filing tool, and it is not tax advice.

t: Something is half business and half personal. What do I do?
b:
Split it by percentage on the transaction. A phone bill at 40% business puts 40% into the Schedule C figure and leaves 60% in your personal budget — and the two never double-count.

This matters more than it sounds. Reading the whole amount instead of the scoped share is how a half-personal purchase becomes a whole deduction, and it is checked by the app's own tests for exactly that reason.

t: What is Fin, and does it send my data anywhere?
b:
Fin is the assistant behind the robot icon. It runs ON YOUR DEVICE using Apple Intelligence and answers from your real numbers.

Nothing you ask leaves your phone. Nothing it reads leaves your phone. There is no request to a server, ours or anybody else's — which is also why it still works with no signal.

It reads the same data the screens do — accounts, transactions, budgets, bills, forecast and plan — and it is bound by the same rules: business money stays out of personal answers, and anything you keep private stays private.

t: What is Fin good at — and what isn't it?
b:
GOOD AT the questions your screens answer slowly: “will I make it to payday?”, “how much can I safely spend?”, “what are my subscriptions?”, “did any go up?”, “what did I spend on dining last month?”, “how am I doing?”. It reads your live figures, so the answer is yours rather than general advice.

NOT GOOD AT anything needing the outside world — it cannot look up a price it hasn't been given, quote tax law, or tell you what a bank charges. It is not a financial adviser and it will not tell you what to buy.

And it can only answer from what you have entered. If your recurring bills are not in the app it cannot know what is coming, and it says so rather than guessing.

t: What can I actually ask Fin?
b:
Plain questions about your own money. Some that work well:

• “Will I make it to payday?”
• “How much can I safely spend today?”
• “What are my subscriptions, and did any go up?”
• “What did I spend on dining last month?”
• “How am I doing?” — it reads your health score and says which pillar is weakest.
• “What is my net worth?” and “how has it moved this year?”
• “Am I balanced?” — your investment allocation against your target.

If it doesn't understand, rephrase around the VERB — “what did I spend” and “what can I spend” are different questions and it treats them that way.

t: Fin gave me an answer I don't believe. What now?
b:
Check it against the screen it came from — Fin reads the same figures you can see, so if the two disagree, one of them is a bug worth reporting.

Most surprises are scope rather than arithmetic: business money is excluded from personal answers, a split contributes only its share, and a transfer between your own accounts is neither income nor spending. “How the numbers work” in this help center walks through all four rules.

If it still looks wrong, Report a Problem with the question you asked and the answer you expected. The question itself is the most useful part.

t: How the Mac app is laid out
b: What does each part of the Mac app do? The sidebar on the left is the whole app. It's grouped by what you're doing — Overview, Money, Planning, Analyze — not by screen name. A group with a triangle expands: Budget holds Monthly, Annual and Categories; Net Worth holds Overview, Investments, Accounts and Projection. ⌘1 through ⌘9 jump straight to the nine screens you'll use most, without touching the sidebar. How-To, Learn and Support are pinned to the bottom of the sidebar, the way Xcode and Music pin theirs. It opens on Home each time — or on Budget, Transactions or Net Worth if you pick one of those as your default in Settings (⌘,). It doesn't reopen wherever you happened to stop.

t: Adding transactions
b: How do I add a transaction? Press ⌘N from anywhere in the app — you don't have to be on Transactions first. Fill in the amount, date, category and account, then save. Transactions ▸ Ledger is the full list. Click Merchant, Date or Amount to sort by it, and click again to reverse. Transactions ▸ Calendar shows the same month as days, which is easier for spotting a heavy week. Made a mistake? Double-click any row in the Ledger to edit it.

t: Budgets — monthly, annual & rings
b: How do I set a budget I'll actually keep? Open Budget ▸ Monthly (⌘2). Each category is a ring: filled is spent, the gap is what's left. Budget ▸ Categories is where you add a category and set its limit. Round numbers are fine to start. Budget ▸ Annual is for the costs that don't arrive monthly — insurance, registration, a yearly subscription. The month selector at the top moves you through history; the rings redraw for whichever month you're looking at. ⇧⌘B opens Budget in its own window, so you can keep it beside the Ledger while you categorize.

t: One-time expenses
b: How do I add or log a one-off expense I already paid for, so it doesn't blow up my monthly budget? A wedding, a ring, a car, a new roof — money you plan once for the YEAR instead of every month. Open Budget ▸ Annual in the sidebar. One-Time Expenses sits below the categories. Click Add and name it. ALREADY BOUGHT IT? Switch on "I've already paid it", enter what it cost and the day you paid — one Save logs the purchase and files it in the year's plan, with no estimate to invent. PLANNING AHEAD instead? Leave that off and enter what you expect it to cost. Click any row to edit or remove it. Either way it counts in the YEAR's plan and never against a monthly budget, so the month you actually pay doesn't go red. Paying later, or in pieces? Tag the payment to it when you enter the transaction. It still counts in cash flow, net worth and every spending report, because the money really did leave your account.

t: Import your data
b: How do I get my existing accounts in? Open Import in the sidebar, under Money. Drag a CSV straight onto the window, or click Browse Files… to pick one. Match your file's columns to date, description, amount and category — the importer guesses, and you correct it. Review the preview before committing. Nothing is written until you confirm. Import is additive and never wipes what's already there, so a second import of an overlapping file is safe to try.

t: Recurring transactions
b: How do I handle bills that repeat every month? Open Transactions ▸ Recurring. Add each bill or paycheck with its amount and how often it repeats. Recurring items feed your forecast and your budget, so a bill you haven't paid yet still shows up in what's ahead. Auto-posting is opt-in and off by default — turn it on only if you want the app to write the transaction for you. Transactions ▸ Rules can categorize incoming transactions automatically by merchant, so you stop re-filing the same coffee shop.

t: Fin — your money assistant
b: Can I just ask a question about my money? Press ⌘K from anywhere to ask Fin a question. Ask about your money — "how much did I spend on groceries last month?" — and Fin answers from your own data. Ask about the app — "how do I split a receipt?" — and Fin quotes the steps from this guide. Fin runs on your device. Your finances aren't sent anywhere to answer a question. When an answer refers to a screen, Fin offers to open it.

t: Where your money goes
b: Where is my money actually going? Open Insights ▸ Spending (⌘7) for the breakdown by category. Insights ▸ Cash Flow shows money in against money out, month by month. Trends compares this month with the months behind it, so a creeping category is visible before it's a problem. Merchants ranks who you actually pay, which is usually more useful than the category. Subscriptions finds the repeating charges hiding in the list.

t: Cover an overspend
b: I went over in one category — can I move budget across? When a category goes over, Budget ▸ Monthly shows it in the red. Open the over-spent category and choose to cover it. Pick the category to move budget FROM. Only categories with room left to give are offered. The amount moves both ways at once — one category's limit goes up, the other's comes down — so your total budget doesn't quietly grow. It's a budget change, not a transaction. Nothing about the actual spending is edited.

t: Find anything fast
b: How do I find one transaction or screen quickly? Press ⌘F to open Find Anything. Type a merchant, an amount, a category or a screen name. Results are grouped, so a transaction, an account and a settings screen matching the same word stay separated. Pick a result and the app goes there — searching is a way to navigate, not just to look. It also finds glossary terms, so searching "amortization" opens the definition rather than a list to scroll.

t: The menu-bar glance
b: Can I check a number without opening the whole app? The app puts a small item in the menu bar at the top of your screen. It's on by default, and can be turned off in Settings. Click it for this month at a glance — left to spend, cash flow and net worth — without bringing the window forward. The rows are also jumps: click one and the main window opens on that screen. It's the fastest way to check a number mid-task, because nothing you're working on gets covered up.

t: Goals & debt payoff
b: How do I set a goal and watch it move? Open Goals (⌘6) in the sidebar under Money. Add a goal with a target amount and, if it has one, a date. Link it to an account and progress tracks your real balance instead of a number you maintain by hand. A debt goal works the same way in reverse — the bar fills as the balance comes down. Each goal shows what it needs per month to land on time, so a date you can't hit is visible now rather than later.

t: Retirement planning
b: Can I model retiring early? Open Retirement ▸ Setup (⌘5) and enter your age, savings and contributions. Retirement ▸ Plan draws the projection; Cash Flow shows the years as income and spending. Analysis stress-tests it — what a worse market, a longer life or an earlier finish does to the plan. Retirement ▸ Report turns the whole thing into a document you can read end to end or print. ⇧⌘P opens the planner in its own window, so you can model against the rest of the app side by side.

t: Reports, printing & exporting
b: How do I share, print or export my numbers? Open Reports (⌘9). Pick a range — this year, last year, or any year you choose — and the sections you want in it. Reports read your historical data too, not just transactions, so a back-filled year isn't blank. ⌘P prints whatever screen is in front. A screen that can't print simply ignores it. Export writes a file you can keep or send. Your numbers never pass through us to get there.

t: Tools & calculators
b: Can I model a loan or a payoff? Open Calculators in the sidebar, under Analyze. Loan and mortgage calculators show what a payment really costs over its life. The payoff calculators compare paying extra now against investing it instead. Taxes (⌘8) estimates what you'll owe from the income and deductions already in the app. Forecast projects your balances forward from your recurring items, so a tight month is visible before it arrives.

t: Investments & retirement accounts
b: How do I track my 401(k) and brokerage? Open Net Worth ▸ Investments (⌘4). Add each holding with its shares and cost basis; prices refresh from the market. A 401(k) or IRA is an account with holdings inside it — add the account first, then what's in it. Allocation shows how your money is split across asset types, which is the number that actually drives risk. Net Worth ▸ Projection grows the whole picture forward at rates you set per bucket.

t: Real estate & rentals
b: How do I track a rental property? Open Net Worth ▸ Accounts and add the property as an asset. Add its mortgage as a liability — net worth counts both, so the equity is what's left. For a rental, log the rent as income and the costs against it, so the property's own profit is separate from your household's. Update the value when you have a real number. The Accounts view flags balances that have gone stale.

t: Mortgages & loans
b: How do I pay a mortgage down faster? Add the loan under Net Worth ▸ Accounts with its balance, rate and payment. The amortisation view splits each payment into interest and principal, which is where the cost actually shows. Add an extra principal amount to see the payoff date and total interest move. Extra payments you've already made are kept as history, so the projection matches what you really did.

t: Sync across your devices
b: How do I use this on my Mac and iPhone together? Sign your Mac and your iPhone into the same Apple ID with iCloud on. Turn on iCloud Sync in Settings (⌘,) on both. Accounts, budgets, goals and plans mirror through your own private iCloud — usually within a minute of a change. It's your iCloud, not our server. We never hold your data. A backup file can be written to iCloud Drive as a second copy, separate from sync.

t: Share with your household
b: How do I share this with my spouse or family? Click the people icon in the window toolbar, top right — Family & Sharing. It has no sidebar row; that toolbar button is the way in. Choose what a read-only summary includes — net worth, budgets, goals — before anyone sees it. Invite them right here: type the email address or phone number on their Apple Account, click Invite, then send them the link with Copy Link or the share button. No iPhone needed at either end — they can be on a Mac too. If you're the one who was invited, this screen shows the household you're in and says so; whoever set it up sends any further invites. MOVING IN TOGETHER? “Combine your finances” runs here too. First it asks which accounts are now ours, then it folds the categories you both kept — and you pick the figure for every row that differs, because summing a rent you both tracked invents money. The household feed and “Who spent what” are on this screen as well: the month split between you, and recent entries with who added each one. Everyone carries their own color, the same color everywhere they appear. Anything you want held back stays held back — transactions, categories, bills, investments, mortgages and retirement plans. Switched off is never sent, not sent-and-hidden.

t: Two windows at once
b: Can I have two screens open side by side? ⇧⌘B opens Budget in its own window; ⇧⌘P opens the Retirement Planner in its own. Either can sit beside the main window, so you can categorize the Ledger while watching the rings move. Each window keeps its own screen — changing one doesn't drag the other along with it. Close an extra window and the main one carries on as it was.

t: Track a business
b: How do I track a business in here too? Turn on business tracking in Settings (⌘,) and a Business section appears in the sidebar. The Mac is the business hub: clients, work log, invoices, receivables, crew, job profit and tax summary all live here. Log work as you go; batch it into invoices at month end from the Month-End Run. ⌘0 jumps to the Business Dashboard once business tracking is on. Business money is kept out of your personal budgets and net worth — the two are scoped separately on purpose.

t: Ask for a feature
b: Can I ask for something the app doesn't do? Open Support at the bottom of the sidebar, and pick Suggest a feature. Say what you were trying to do — that is more useful than a feature name, because it leaves room for a better answer than the one you had in mind. Send it from here rather than by email: the message keeps its thread, and the reply comes back into Your messages inside the app. Diagnostics is there if something is broken — versions, sync state and record counts, with no transaction detail in it. This app is built by one person, and a specific request from someone using it daily is the single best thing you can send.

t: Your financial health score
b: Am I actually doing all right? Open Health Score in the sidebar, under Overview. One number out of 100, with a letter grade beside it. It blends five pillars: emergency fund (months of expenses in cash), savings rate (income kept over the last 90 days), debt load (non-mortgage debt against annual income), net worth, and budget adherence. The pillars are weighted by impact, so the fastest way up is whichever one is lowest — that is what Do this next lists, in order. Every card links to the screen that changes it. Click Open Accounts, Open Forecast or Open Goals to go and act on it rather than reading about it. Retirement pace is not scored until you set a birthday and an income in Settings ▸ Profile. Everything is computed on your Mac from data already in the app.

t: Subscriptions & recurring charges
b: What am I paying for every month without noticing? Open Subscriptions in the sidebar. Nothing to enter — it reads your transaction history and finds charges from the same merchant that repeat on a rhythm. It works out the cadence, predicts the next charge, and puts a badge on anything whose price has gone up. Repeating is not the same as billing: a weekly grocery run repeats too. The detector measures how STEADY the amount is, so a fixed £11.99 is a subscription and a £40-to-£210 supermarket shop is not. Click Track on any of them to turn it into a real recurring bill, which then feeds your Budget and your Forecast. The recurring manager underneath is where you edit cadence, amount and reminders once something is tracked.

t: Cash-flow forecast
b: Will I make it to payday? Open Forecast under Planning. It takes today's cash, adds the income due, subtracts the bills due, and draws the balance forward day by day. Safe to spend today is the headline: what you can spend now without the projection dipping below your buffer before the horizon. Set the safety buffer to the cushion you never want to go under. Safe-to-spend and the negative-balance warning both respect it. Lowest point is the day to watch. If it goes red, the fix is usually to move money in or push one bill — the warning says which. Include savings accounts decides whether the projection may lean on savings. Leave it off if that money is not really available.

t: Asset allocation & rebalancing
b: Is my portfolio still the shape I chose? Open Allocation in the sidebar. The donut is what you hold today; the Target mix sliders are what you want to hold. Set your target mix — US stocks, international, bonds, real estate, cash, crypto. The total has to reach 100%, and the card tells you when it does. Current vs target shows the drift per class, and the summary at the top names the biggest one. To rebalance is the total of the moves needed. The portfolio map sizes every holding by value and colors it by class, which is the fastest way to see a position that has quietly grown too large. Tickers are classified automatically. Anything it gets wrong can be overridden per holding, and the mix updates immediately. Include cash accounts decides whether cash counts as part of the portfolio. This is arithmetic against a target you set, not investment advice.

t: Spending trends over time
b: Is my spending getting better or worse? Open Trends under Analyze. This is the long view — Insights explains this month, Trends compares it with the months before it. The spending heatmap is one square per day over the recent weeks. Darker is heavier, and a bad stretch shows up as a block rather than a number. Unusual this month lists any category running meaningfully above its own recent average, projected to full-month pace — so early in a month those are estimates. Savings rate is income minus expenses as a share of income, tracked month over month. It needs income recorded to show anything. Where it goes over time stacks the categories, so you can see composition change even when the total does not.

t: Everyone you paid
b: Which shops am I spending the most at? Open Merchants under Analyze. Every merchant you have paid, ranked by total — with how often, how much, and which way the trend is going. It shows the top 60; search narrows the list rather than paging through it. This is the screen for the question budgets cannot answer: not "how much on groceries", but "how much at this one shop". A merchant that keeps landing in the wrong category is a rule waiting to be written — Transactions ▸ Rules does it once for every future transaction. Click through any merchant to see the transactions behind its total.

t: Auto-categorization rules
b: Can it stop asking me to categorize the same shop? Open Transactions ▸ Rules. A rule matches a merchant and files the transaction for you, so the same shop never has to be categorized twice. Match by contains, starts with or is exactly — contains is right nearly always, because card statements append store numbers and cities. New transactions are filed as they arrive. "Apply to Uncategorized" runs every enabled rule over transactions that have no category yet — which is how a new rule catches up with an import. It deliberately leaves anything you have already categorized alone. A rule should never overwrite a decision you made by hand. The switch on a rule enables and disables it without deleting it, which is how you test whether a rule is the thing causing a surprise. Rules are the cure for the most common import complaint: everything landed in the wrong category. Fix it once here instead of row by row.

t: Year in Review
b: How did the whole year actually go? Open Year in Review under Overview. Three views: This Year, Year by Year, and Month over Month. This Year is the summary — what came in, what went out, what was kept, and the categories that moved most. Year by Year lists every year on record, including ones you back-filled by importing old statements. Click a row to open that year. Month over Month puts the twelve months side by side, which is where a seasonal pattern becomes obvious. ⌘P prints whatever you are looking at, which is the quickest way to keep a copy at tax time.

t: Taxes & deductions
b: What is this going to cost me in tax? Open Taxes (⌘8). Three views: Estimator for this year's bill, Lifetime for the tax your retirement plan projects bracket by bracket, and Deductions for what is claimable. The estimator uses the income and the plan already in the app, so it moves when your figures do rather than being a form you re-fill. Deductions gathers what the app already knows is deductible — mortgage interest, business expenses, mileage — instead of asking you to remember them in April. Reports ▸ Tax Preparation Pack prints the same figures with the rentals and mortgage interest attached, which is the version to hand to a preparer. These are estimates from your own numbers, not filing advice.

t: Make it all agree with the bank
b: My balance here doesn't match my bank. Now what? Open Net Worth and click Reconcile in the toolbar. One sheet, every account, with your bank tabs open beside it. Type what each account really says today. Blank rows are left alone, so you can do the three that matter and ignore the rest. The difference is written as a balance adjustment rather than by rewriting history — your past transactions stay exactly as they were. Investments reconcile by SHARE COUNT, not value. A correction is added at your average cost so the return you have earned does not move. Reconcile All applies the lot and records a net-worth snapshot at the same time, which is what puts the point on your trajectory chart. Doing this once a month is the whole maintenance routine for an app that is not linked to a bank.

t: Where your net worth is heading
b: What does this look like in ten years? Open Net Worth ▸ Projection. It carries your current net worth forward using what you save and what your debts do. The trajectory is built from your own snapshots, so it gets more honest the longer you have been recording them — and Reconcile is what records them.
