Change the assumptions to see the shape change; the milestone years underneath move with it. Include a spouse or partner to project the household rather than one person. This is a projection from your figures, not a promise about markets.

t: Compare with friends
b: Can I see how I compare with anyone? Open Friends in the sidebar. It compares a few numbers you choose — savings rate, a utility bill, the month's income — with people you invite. Nothing is shared until you switch it on, and you pick which numbers individually. Everyone chooses their own. It works between Apple devices signed in to iCloud with Simple Finance installed. There is no Android or web version, so an invitation only reaches people who have the app. Balances and transactions are never part of it — only the specific figures you turned on. Turn any of them back off and it stops being shared straight away.

t: How the app is laid out
b: What does each part of the app do? Home is your dashboard — this month's cash flow, budgets, goals and the year so far, all at a glance. Transactions is every bit of money in and out. Budget is what you planned to spend, by category. Net Worth totals what you own minus what you owe. Plan is the retirement planner and the calculators. The ☰ button top-left opens everything else — goals, bills, reports, settings and this guide.

t: Adding transactions
b: How do I add a transaction? On the Transactions tab, tap the + button in the bottom-right corner. Pick Expense, Income or Transfer along the top, then enter the amount, the merchant and a category. Attach a receipt while you’re there, or snap one later — it reads the merchant, amount and date for you to approve. Splitting a bill? Turn on “Split this bill” and set how many people. Enter the FULL total — only your share is recorded.

t: Budgets — monthly, annual & rings
b: How do I set a budget I’ll actually keep? The Budget tab opens on this month. LEFT TO SPEND is the whole screen in one number — your budgets minus what you've spent. Tap the month in the title bar for the period picker: Monthly or Annual, any month of any year, and “Customize This Month” for a different amount just this once. The ‹ › arrows step a month at a time — a year at a time in Annual. The tiles below the ring are your categories. One over budget turns red and offers Cover, which moves the difference from a category with room to spare rather than pretending the month was fine. Tap a tile for that category on its own: what it went on, the merchants, every transaction, and Edit budget right there. Tap an ARC of the ring instead and the ring itself focuses — the middle switches to that category and a strip appears beneath it. The small toggle by the ring flips the tiles between bars and rings, and “See all…” opens the full list. Set a category's budget when you add or edit it, and give it any color you like. Half of them still unbudgeted? A “Set up your budget” card walks every one and suggests amounts from what you actually spend. ANNUAL is the same screen for a whole year — each category against its yearly budget, with income and spending year to date. One-Time Expenses live there too: a wedding, a ring, a car. They count in the YEAR's plan and never in a monthly budget, so the month you actually pay doesn't turn red. Any transaction can be tagged to one.

t: One-time expenses
b: How do I add or log a one-off expense I already paid for, so it doesn’t blow up my monthly budget? A wedding, a ring, a car, a new roof — money you plan once for the YEAR instead of every month. Budget tab → tap the month in the title bar → Annual. Scroll to One-Time Expenses and tap “Add a One-Time Expense”. ALREADY BOUGHT IT? Turn on “I’ve already paid it”, then just enter what it cost and the day you paid. One Save logs the purchase AND files it in the year’s plan — no estimate to invent. PLANNING AHEAD instead? Leave that off and enter what you expect it to cost, plus the month it lands in if you know it. Either way it counts in the YEAR’s plan and never against a monthly budget, so the month you actually pay doesn’t turn red. Paying for it later, or in pieces? On an expense, set One-Time Expense on the transaction to point it at the plan — or tap “New one-time expense…” right there and create one without leaving the form. It still counts everywhere else — cash flow, net worth, spending reports and year to date all include it, because the money really did leave your account.

t: Import your data
b: How do I get my existing accounts in? Open ☰ → Import, or tap + on the Net Worth tab. ACCOUNTS & LOANS: type them in, or snap a photo of an account list, balance sheet or spreadsheet — each line is read and classified as a home, car, investment, loan and so on. A CSV (Name, Type, Balance) works too, with a template to copy. INVESTMENTS & CRYPTO: holdings, share counts and cost basis. TRANSACTIONS: a CSV or OFX/QFX export from your bank. PAST YEARS: totals from before you started the app, so the year views go back further. Whichever you pick, there are the same three ways in: type it in, snap a PHOTO of a statement, or load a SPREADSHEET. Everything is reviewed before it’s saved — nothing is written until you approve the list, and the whole batch can be undone straight after.

t: Recurring transactions
b: How do I handle bills that repeat every month? Open ☰ → Recurring. Tap + (top right) to add one: merchant, amount, category, income vs expense, and the day of the month it’s due. The calendar shows every bill and payday for the month, so you can see what’s coming before it lands. Optional: turn on Auto-Post in Settings to log them automatically each month. Off by default — you stay in control.

t: Fin — your money assistant
b: Can I just ask a question about my money? Tap Fin’s face at the top RIGHT of the Home screen. Ask anything in plain English — “How am I doing this month?”, “What did I spend on dining last year?”, “Can I afford $300 more in savings?” Or tap the microphone and just say it. Ask for a chart (“chart income vs spending for 2024 and 2025”) and Fin builds it from your real numbers. Fin opens on Insights it worked out already — whether you’re on track, what’s trending over, your biggest one-off. Ask for a month or year report, or let Fin suggest money moves you can apply with a tap. It all runs ON YOUR DEVICE with Apple Intelligence — your finances never leave your phone. Siri works too.

t: Where your money goes
b: Where is my money actually going? Open ☰ → Spending Insights, or tap “See where your money goes” on Home. Switch the range at the top — 1, 3, 6 or 12 months — to see a trend rather than a single month. The card leads with the total, your average day, and the same figure last month — then what you’re ON PACE to finish at, so you hear about a bad month while you can still do something about it. The 6-month trend bars show whether this month is normal for you. Touch and hold a bar for that month’s total. Top Categories and Top Merchants tell you where it actually went, not just how much. Keep scrolling for Biggest Movers — what changed most against last month, right in red for more, left in green for less — then Biggest Purchases and Compare Years. The ⓘ on any card explains how its number is worked out.

t: Cover an overspend
b: I went over in one category — can I move budget across? Go over in a category and it turns red on the Budget tab — bar full and past the end, or a ring over 100%. A “Cover … from …” chip appears on that row. Tap it. The sheet leads with exactly what you’re short. It suggests the category with the most genuinely SPARE money — a large budget that’s still going to be spent doesn’t win. Pick a different one if you’d rather; only what’s actually unspent is offered. Set the amount — All, Half, or your own — and “After this move” shows both categories’ new budgets before you commit. The row then says where the money came from, with an Undo beside it. The move applies to THIS MONTH only — next month goes back to your usual budgets. Nothing single has enough? The sheet offers to split it across several categories in one tap. You can also start from the ⌄ menu → Move Money Between Categories, which lists every category, not just the ones already over.

t: Find anything fast
b: How do I find one transaction or screen quickly? Open ☰ and tap the search field at the top. Search transactions by merchant, note or category — typing “housing” finds everything in that category, not just merchants named it. It also finds accounts, goals, categories, every screen in the app, and the whole Learn library. Tap any result to go straight there.

t: Goals & debt payoff
b: How do I set a goal and watch it move? On Home, tap + on the Goals card — or open ☰ → Goals. Save Up: set a target, then link transfers to it to build progress. Pay Down — the second tab at the top: link a mortgage, auto loan or other debt account and progress tracks itself as the balance drops. Pay extra principal: add a Transfer, set its type to “Extra Principal”, and link it to the goal. Tap any goal for its own screen — progress, pace, projected finish, and a photo if you want one. Tap any goal for its own screen — what’s saved, what’s left, what it needs per month, and when it lands at the pace you’re actually going. Add a photo and it becomes the header.

t: Reports & exporting
b: How do I share or export my numbers? Open ☰ → Reports for the Report Studio. Pick a report: Complete Financial Report, Net Worth Statement, Income & Spending, Budget Performance, Investment Portfolio, Budget to Share, Retirement Readiness, Tax Preparation Pack, Debt & Payoff or Subscription Audit. Choose a period, then tick the pages you want. Pages with no data for that period are dimmed and left out. SENDING IT TO SOMEONE? Use “Budget to Share”, or the “Hide everything that shows balances” button — the cover prints your net worth otherwise. Preview every page, then export as a PDF. Settings → Full Backup saves everything separately.

t: Tools & calculators
b: Can I model a loan, a payoff or retiring early? Open ☰ → Calculators. Eighteen of them, grouped by the job: Buy a Home, Kill Debt, Save & Invest, Income & Spending. Mortgage, refinance, rent vs buy, debt payoff, credit card, student loan, auto, compound interest, FIRE, Roth vs Traditional, take-home pay and more. Every one leads with the answer and charts it, so you can see the shape and not just the number. Save any calculation to revisit or tweak it later.

t: Net worth, investments & retirement
b: How do I track my net worth, 401(k) and brokerage? The Net Worth tab opens on Overview: everything you own against everything you owe, with this month and the year so far underneath. The history chart below runs 3M to All, or a range you pick. The Stocks segment is the investing half. One card totals every investment account and what it has returned; the refresh, history and + buttons sit on it. Add an account — Brokerage, Roth or Traditional IRA, SEP/SIMPLE, 401(k), 403(b), 457, TSP, HSA or 529 — then add holdings by ticker (AAPL, VTI, VOO) and share count. Give an account its own icon and color if you like. Each holding row shows a chart of today’s session beside its figure. The header pill switches what that figure MEANS — market value, today’s change, or total return — for every list at once, and it remembers. Tap a holding for its own screen: a real chart from a day to five years, your cost basis and lots, dividends, and pre-market or after-hours prices when the market is shut. Stocks & Funds charts the whole portfolio over the same ranges. It prices your CURRENT shares at past prices — it is what you hold, valued back through time, not a record of past trades. On a retirement or HSA account, enter what you’ve contributed this year and see it against the IRS limit. Auto-invest plans log recurring buys against the account they land in. Crypto works the same way in its own section, priced per coin. A mutual fund has no intraday price at all, so its row says “at last NAV” rather than pretending the figure is today’s. The Watchlist follows a ticker you don’t own — those never count toward your net worth. “vs Market” puts your portfolio against the S&P 500, the Dow and the NASDAQ over a week to a year — so a good month is a good month RELATIVE to something.

t: Real estate & rentals
b: How do I track a rental property? On the Net Worth tab, tap + → Add Account → Rental Property (residential, multi-family, short-term, commercial or land). Enter the value, monthly rent, operating expenses and attach a mortgage — equity is worked out for you. Tap the property for full analytics: cash flow, cap rate, cash-on-cash, the 1% rule, total ROI, appreciation and tax depreciation. Optional: auto value updates appreciate (or depreciate) at a rate you set — or update by hand any time. Tag transactions to a property to track its real income and expenses for the year.

t: Mortgages & loans
b: How do I track a mortgage and pay it down faster? On the Net Worth tab, tap + and add a liability — Mortgage, Auto, Credit Card, HELOC, Personal, Medical, Tax, Business or other. For a mortgage, tap it and choose “Set Up Loan”: interest rate, term, monthly payment, property tax, insurance, PMI and any extra principal. You get a full payment breakdown — principal, interest, tax, insurance — plus amortisation and payoff projections. Auto-Pay applies the scheduled principal each month for you. Interest and principal recalculate from the live balance, so an extra payment lowers next month’s interest. Extra principal you pay is recorded against the loan AND the account, so the balance and the history agree. The Debt & Loan Payoff report page lists every loan, its cost and when it clears.

t: Sync across your devices
b: How do I use this on my iPad and Mac too? Settings → iCloud Sync. It is OFF by default — your data stays on this device until you turn it on. Once on, accounts, transactions, budgets and goals sync through your own private iCloud to every device on your Apple ID. There’s a Mac app too, and it’s the same purchase — not a separate one to buy. Search the Mac App Store for Simple Finance, sign in with the same Apple Account, and turn this on. Everything you’ve entered on your phone is already there. Changing this takes effect after you restart the app. It’s your private database — nothing is shared with us, and it’s separate from iCloud Sharing with family.

t: Share with your household
b: How do I share this with my spouse or family? Tap the two-people button at the top of Home. That’s Sharing — who you share with, what they see, and whether it’s up to date. Nobody yet? “Invite someone” asks one question first — partner, family or friend — because those are three different things, not three sizes of the same thing. PARTNER: a shared ledger. Name them, send the invite, and Live Two-Way Sync turns itself on — on your phone when you send it, on theirs when they accept. The switch is there if you ever want it off. FAMILY: a read-only summary instead. You tick what it includes — anything switched off is never sent, not just hidden — and they can never edit anything. FRIENDS: fewer numbers still. You pick which ones — savings rate, a utility bill, the month’s income — and nothing is shared until you do. Whichever you pick, “See exactly what they will see” shows you their view of you, built from your real numbers, before you send anything. Once it’s live everyone is in one list, each row saying what flows which way. Tap anyone to change just that person — see “Who sees what”. MOVING IN TOGETHER? “Combine your finances” on the Sharing screen is one pass through the awkward part. First it asks which accounts are now OURS — anything you leave off stays yours, and so does every transaction that touches it. Then it folds the categories you both kept. Rent tracked on two phones becomes one line, and you pick the figure yourself for every row that differs — the larger, the smaller, or both added together. Nothing is chosen for you, because adding up a rent you both tracked invents money that was never spent. Categories that are shared BY NATURE — rent, groceries, utilities — arrive already marked as household, so you are not ticking them one at a time. Anything personal you can hold back. “Kept private” reaches further than it used to: individual transactions and categories, and also bills, investments, mortgages and retirement plans. Something switched off is never sent — not sent-and-hidden. Your home-screen layout stays personal to each of you. Your COLOR does not — see “Who sees what”.

t: Who sees what
b: How do I control who can see what, and change what one person sees? The two-people button at the top of Home opens People — everyone you share with, in one list. Each row names the access level, and the two small chips underneath say which way it flows: what comes IN to you, and what goes OUT to them. Tap anyone to open just that relationship. Everything about them is on that one screen — there is no second place to go. Your partner opens your household: what each of you spent this month, what either of you bought recently, Notes, what you’re keeping back, and your colors and pictures. Family and friends open a two-sided screen instead. Their tab is the card they sent you; the You tab is exactly what they see of you, built from your real numbers rather than described. The You tab is also where you change it — net worth, income, the accounts behind it, investments, goals, bills, a six-month trend. Or narrow it further and pick the individual categories and bills, one at a time. Switching something off removes it from their device. It isn’t left out of the next update — it goes. Everyone in a household carries their own color and picture, and it is the same color in every place a person appears — the dot on a transaction, the feed, the split bar. After a day of it you stop reading names. “Who spent what” on the Sharing screen splits the month between you, and the feed underneath lists what either of you added recently, each row saying who added it. On Transactions you can filter to Mine, Theirs or Joint. “Joint” means a shared expense, not “unknown” — with one exception: rows entered before the app started recording who added them have no author, and those say Joint too. Want to try it first? Settings → Privacy & Security → Demo Mode gives you sample people and live switches. Nothing you touch in there reaches a real share.

t: Privacy, security & demo
b: How do I turn on Face ID, or hide amounts when someone picks up my phone? Your data lives on your device and in your own private iCloud — never on our servers. Settings → Privacy & Security: require Face ID to open the whole app, or just to view Net Worth — one or the other, and turning either off needs Face ID as well. Hide Sensitive Amounts blurs money on screen so you can hand your phone to someone; “What to Hide” decides how much. Revealing needs Face ID, and the eye button on Home toggles it in one tap. Hide When App Is Backgrounded covers the app in the app switcher, so a screenshot of your task list never shows balances. Reports and exports always contain the real numbers. Showing the app to someone? Demo Mode swaps in realistic sample data — your real numbers stay hidden and untouched, and “Require Face ID to Exit Demo” stops them switching back.

t: Customize your dashboard
b: Can I change what’s on my home screen? On Home, scroll to the bottom and tap “Customize Dashboard”. Drag the handle to reorder a section, or tap − to hide it. The header at the top always stays put. “Add a Widget” below has the ones you’re not showing — Left to Spend, Budget Rings, Money Flow and more. Tap + to put one on. Your Home screen, your order. It doesn’t change anyone else’s in a shared household.

t: Notifications & smart alerts
b: How do I get told before something goes wrong? Settings → Notifications, then tap “Enable Notifications” to allow them. Budget alerts fire the moment a category crosses your threshold, and again if you go over. Bill reminders fire a chosen number of days before each recurring expense is due. Goal Milestones cheer you on at 50%, 75% and when you get there. Weekly Fin Check-In sends Fin’s top insight on Sunday mornings. Smart Money Alerts add optional nudges: cash-flow warnings near month-end, leftover cash worth saving, unusual spending in a category, and large purchases. Everything is opt-in and each alert is sent once. “Send a Test Notification” shows you what one looks like.

t: Make it yours
b: Can I change the colors and categories? Settings → Appearance: pick an accent color, or any custom color, to re-tint the app. Green is the default. Choose Light, Dark or System, and set your display currency — it changes how amounts are shown and never converts what you stored. “Show whole dollars” rounds the display; you can still enter cents. App Icon swaps the home-screen icon: Classic is the bars-and-trend mark, Ring echoes the planner’s chance-of-success dial. Give each budget category its own color and icon — it flows through to charts, rings, reports and widgets. Income green and overspend red never change, whatever accent you pick, so a color always means the same thing. Add a widget: long-press your iPhone Home Screen → + → Simple Finance, then pick what it shows.

t: Track a business
b: How do I track a business in here too? Business tracking is OFF until you ask for it — nothing about the app changes for people who don't run one. Settings → Business, then turn on “Track a business separately”. A Business row appears in the ☰ panel. Add your business: a name, a type (sole trader, LLC, S-corp) and, if you invoice, an address and logo. A Personal / Business switch appears in the toolbar. Everything — budgets, reports, net worth — filters to whichever side you're on. Tag transactions to the business as you go, or bulk-assign later. Deductible categories map to Schedule C lines. Once it's on, a full Business guide appears inside the Business screen, covering invoices, mileage, deductions and the tax summary.

t: Ask for a feature
b: Can I ask for something the app doesn't do? ☰ → Help & Support → Suggest a feature. Say what you were TRYING TO DO, not just the feature name — “I wanted to see how much I spent at one shop this year” is more useful than “add merchant reports”, because it might already be possible. Tap one of the starters if the blank box is the hard part. They’re just first sentences; edit freely. It sends from inside the app, and the reply lands in Your messages on the same screen. Nothing about your finances is attached. A real person reads them, and a good number of them ship.

t: Find your subscriptions
b: What am I paying for every month without noticing? ☰ → Tools → Subscriptions. Nothing to enter — it reads your history and finds charges from the same merchant that repeat on a rhythm. It works out the cadence, predicts the next charge, and badges anything whose price has gone up. Repeating is not the same as billing: a weekly shop repeats too. The detector measures how STEADY the amount is, so a fixed $11.99 is a subscription and a variable supermarket shop is not. Tap Track to turn one into a real recurring bill, which then feeds your Budget. This is usually the fastest money the app finds you — people cancel something on this screen more often than on any other.

t: Stop categorizing the same shop
b: Can it stop asking me to categorize the same shop? ☰ → Rules. A rule matches a merchant and files the transaction for you. Match by contains, starts with or is exactly — contains is right nearly always, because card statements append store numbers and cities. New transactions are filed as they arrive. “Apply to Uncategorized” runs every enabled rule over transactions that have no category yet — which is how a new rule catches up with an import. Anything you have already categorized is left alone. The switch on a rule turns it off without deleting it, which is how you test whether a rule is causing a surprise. Rules are the cure for the most common import complaint: everything landed in the wrong category. Fix it once here instead of row by row.

t: Taxes & deductions
b: What is this going to cost me in tax? ☰ → Tools. Two of them: Tax Estimator works out this year's bill, and Tax Center tracks what is deductible. The estimator uses the income and the plan already in the app, so it moves when your figures do rather than being a form you re-fill. Deductions gathers what the app already knows is claimable — mortgage interest, business expenses, mileage — instead of asking you to remember them in April. Reports → Tax Preparation Pack prints the same figures with rentals and mortgage interest attached; that is the version to hand a preparer. These are estimates from your own numbers, not filing advice.

t: Make it all agree with the bank
b: My balance here doesn't match my bank. Now what? Net Worth → Reconcile. One screen, every account, with your bank app open beside it. Type what each account really says today. Blank rows are left alone, so you can do the three that matter and ignore the rest. The difference is written as a balance adjustment rather than by rewriting history — your past transactions stay exactly as they were. Investments reconcile by SHARE COUNT, not value. A correction is added at your average cost so the return you have earned does not move. Reconcile All applies the lot and records a net-worth snapshot at the same time, which is what puts the point on your trajectory chart. Once a month is the whole maintenance routine.

t: The app crashed or closed by itself
b:
Reopen it. Nothing is lost — every change is written as you make it, not when you leave the screen, so you come back to exactly what you had.

If it happens more than once, the useful thing is not a log, it is a sentence: WHICH screen you were on and WHAT you had just clicked. That one line is usually enough to find it.

Send it with Report a Problem and leave “Attach device info” on. That sends versions, settings and how many records you have — never transactions, names or amounts.

Two things that are NOT a fault:
• Turning Demo Mode on or off writes or clears hundreds of rows. It can sit still for a few seconds; clicking again during that starts it over.
• iOS closes apps in the background all the time to free memory. Reopening after a few hours and finding it back at the start is normal, not a crash.

t: The app is slow, or a screen won't respond
b:
Force-quit and reopen first. It clears a stuck screen and touches none of your data.

Where slowness is real and expected:
• A tab that shows balances recomputes them from your transactions when it opens. With years of history that is a beat, not a hang.
• The Transactions CALENDAR does more work than the list for a heavy month — the list is the faster way to scan.
• The first iCloud sync after switching it on is the slow one; later changes land in seconds.
• Prices refresh when you open Investments, so that screen has a moment of work on arrival.

If ONE screen is always slow and the rest are fine, that is worth reporting — name the screen and roughly how many transactions you have. “The app is slow” is very hard to act on; “Budget takes 4 seconds with 12,000 transactions” is a bug report.

t: A screen is blank, or a number looks wrong
b:
Check the scope first. The pill at the top of Home and Transactions switches between Personal, Business and Everything, and it is remembered across tabs — a business with no activity this month renders honest zeroes that look exactly like data loss.

Then check the period. Most figures name theirs (“this month”, “2026 year to date”); if a number surprises you, read the label under it before assuming it is wrong.

Still wrong? Send us the screen name, the figure you see and the figure you expected. Two numbers and a screen name is the fastest bug report there is.

t: My account balance didn't move after importing
b:
Two switches, and the app looks reasonable without either.

1. On the import screen, “Import into” must name the account. It starts on your default account now; on “No account” the transactions import but belong to nothing, so no balance can follow them.
2. On the account, “Track balance from transactions” must be on. New checking, savings and cash accounts set this for you; older accounts kept the balance you typed.

Already imported without an account? Select the rows in Transactions and set the account — the balance recomputes from your starting figure, so nothing double-counts.

Not a fault: an opening balance never shows in Year in Review. It is a starting position, not income.

t: My iPhone and Mac aren't in sync
b:
Work through these in order.

1. Both devices signed into the SAME Apple ID, and iCloud Sync switched on in Settings on each one — it is off until you turn it on, and turning it on takes effect after the app restarts.
2. Both online. Sync is not a background magic trick; the app has to be open at least once on each side.
3. Give it a minute. The first mirror after turning sync on is the slow one — later changes usually land within seconds.
4. Still nothing? Settings → iCloud Sync shows the sync status and the last error, if there was one. That message is the fastest thing to send us.

One thing that is NOT a fault: a device you haven't opened in a while shows old numbers until you open it. Nothing syncs to an app that isn't running.

t: Investment prices look out of date
b:
Prices refresh when you open Net Worth → Investments, and you can force it with Refresh Prices there.

Some things that look wrong are not:
• A mutual fund has NO intraday price. It is valued once after the close, so it legitimately sits still while stocks move.
• Before the market opens, a day change refers to the previous session — not the one that hasn't started.
• Weekends and holidays hold Friday's close.

If a real stock is genuinely stale, check your connection and refresh the screen. Manual accounts never auto-update; they hold whatever balance you typed.

t: An imported transaction is wrong
b: Imports are review-first — double-click any transaction to edit the amount, category, or type. Set up a Rule (Transactions → Rules) to auto-fix similar ones going forward.

t: The app keeps asking for Touch ID or your Apple Watch or a password
b:
App Lock is on — Settings → Privacy & Security. You can turn it off there, or change when it asks.

If it asks EVERY time you switch apps for a second, that is the lock doing its job on returning from the background. If it fails repeatedly, the system falls back to your Mac login password; the app never sees either one, it only gets a yes or no from the system.

t: My balances show as dots or are hidden
b:
Hide Amounts is on. It blurs every figure in the app in one click, for when somebody is looking over your shoulder.

Turn it off from the sidebar (Hide Amounts) or in Settings → Privacy & Security. It is per-device and never syncs, so hiding on your phone does not hide on your Mac.

Nothing is deleted or changed while it is on — it is a blur over the display, not a setting that touches your data.

t: iCloud Sync won't turn on
b:
The switch needs an iCloud account signed in on the device and iCloud Drive enabled for the app in System Settings. If it turns itself back off, the app couldn't start the sync engine — Settings → iCloud Sync shows the reason underneath, and that sentence is the useful thing to send us.

Your data is never at risk while this is happening: the app falls back to a local database and keeps working.

t: My partner can't see what I share
b:
Check, in this order:

1. They accepted the invitation — an unaccepted invite looks identical to a broken share from your side.
2. Both of you have iCloud Sync on. Household sharing rides on it.
3. The thing itself isn't kept private. Anything marked private is removed from their device by design.
4. They've opened the app since you made the change. Nothing arrives on a device that hasn't been opened.

Business money is never shared, no matter the setting.

t: We both have the same category twice
b: That happens when you each created a category with the same name before you started sharing — they are two different categories that happen to read alike. Open the sidebar → Family & Sharing → Review what you share, and choose which budget to keep for each duplicated name. Merging keeps the transactions from both.

t: A recurring bill didn't post
b:
Recurring items post when the app is opened on or after the due day, and only when Auto-Post Recurring is on (Settings → Transactions). If it is off, nothing posts until you log the bill yourself.

Also check the bill isn't paused, and that its next due date is what you expect — a bill edited mid-month keeps its own schedule.

t: A bill posted twice
b:
This should not happen — postings are matched to the bill and its period specifically to prevent it. If you have two, the usual cause is two copies of the same BILL, which can happen after restoring a backup. Delete the duplicate bill (not the transactions) and the doubling stops.

If you find a genuine double from a single bill, that is a defect and worth reporting — it's the kind we fix quickly.

t: My import didn't read the file
b:
Export the file again as CSV if you can — an Excel file saved as "Unicode Text" or an unusual encoding is the most common cause. The app tries the common encodings in order and should cope with accented characters.

If the columns landed in the wrong place, the preview is there to catch it before anything saves. And if a file simply won't read, send it to us through Report a Problem — a real file is worth more than a description of one.

t: An imported amount is wrong or zero
b:
Check the preview before saving — every row is shown first for exactly this reason. Amounts wrapped in parentheses, with currency symbols, or using a comma as the decimal mark are all handled, but an unusual export can still confuse a column.

A row that shows as zero when it shouldn't is worth reporting with the file attached; an amount the app couldn't read should never be saved as a number.

t: My budget total doesn't match the Home screen
b:
The most common cause is the period: Home shows this month, and a budget category may be on a yearly limit.

After that, check for split transactions — a split counts only its share toward each category, which is correct but can look short if you were expecting the whole amount. If business mode is on, personal totals deliberately exclude business spending.

t: A goal isn't updating
b:
A goal moves when money is recorded against it. Link the goal to the account or the recurring transfer that funds it, and contributions count automatically; otherwise it only changes when you add to it by hand.

If a linked goal still isn't moving, check that the funding transactions are dated in the past — future-dated rows are scheduled, not banked.

t: I'm not getting notifications
b:
Two switches have to agree: System Settings → Notifications → Simple Finance must be allowed, and the specific reminders have to be on in Settings → Notifications inside the app.

Everything is scheduled on your device, so nothing about your money is sent anywhere to make a reminder happen — which also means a device that is off or has the app deleted simply won't fire them.

t: My widget shows old numbers
b:
Widgets are refreshed by iOS on its own schedule, not on demand, so a short lag is normal. Opening the app updates the data the widget reads from.

If a widget seems stuck for a long time, remove it and add it back — a placed widget keeps its own configuration, and re-adding is the only way to reset it.

t: It says my data is running locally
b:
The app couldn't start iCloud sync, so it fell back to a local database to avoid losing anything — everything still works, it just isn't mirroring.

Settings → iCloud Sync shows the exact reason underneath. The most common one is an Apple Account that needs re-verifying in System Settings. Nothing is lost while this is happening, and sync resumes on its own once the account is healthy.

t: A number looks wrong somewhere
b:
Almost every figure is derived from your transactions and balances for the period on screen, so start with the period selector at the top — a month view and a year view of the same category are supposed to differ.

Then check the usual three:
• A SPLIT transaction only counts its share toward each category.
• A TRANSFER between your own accounts is deliberately not income or spending.
• If business mode is on, personal figures exclude business money, and the other way round.

If it still doesn't add up, send it through Report a Problem with the screen and the number you expected — attach the device info and we can usually see it from here.

t: The numbers someone shares with me are hours old
b:
This is usually not a fault. A summary is published by THEIR device, in the foreground — so the age you are looking at is the time since they last opened the app, not the time since yours checked.

If they haven't opened it since yesterday morning, yesterday morning is the freshest figure that exists. Nothing you do on your side can pull a newer one.

What IS worth checking: that they still appear in your People list with a live status, and that both of you are online. Refreshing the People screen asks iCloud again.

t: My widget ignores the metric I picked in the app
b:
A placed widget keeps its OWN configuration. Changing the default inside the app does not reach a widget already sitting on your desktop or in Notification Center.

Right-click the widget → Edit Widget, and set it there. If the option you want isn't offered, remove the widget and add it again — a re-added widget picks up the current set of choices.

t: A stock price won't refresh
b:
Prices come from a public market source with rate limits, and a burst of refreshes can get you held off for a few minutes. Waiting is the fix; hammering refresh is not.

Things that look like a stale price and aren't:
• A MUTUAL FUND has no intraday price at all — one NAV after the close, and it legitimately sits still all day.
• BEFORE THE OPENING BELL there is no session yet, so the day change belongs to the previous one. The row says “at close” when that is what you are looking at.
• Weekends and market holidays hold Friday's close.

A manual account never updates on its own; it holds whatever balance you typed.

t: I restored a backup and now everything is doubled
b:
That is what restoring on top of existing data does, and it is fixable in one screen.

Settings → Data & Backup → Repair Duplicated Records. It looks for the same RECORD present as several rows — which only a re-import or a restore can produce — and shows you what it found before it removes anything. Duplicate accounts, categories, subcategories and businesses are all on that screen too.

Run it once and rescan; nothing is lost and no money is double-counted afterwards.

t: Demo Mode won't turn off, or sample data is still here
b:
Demo Mode is a switch: Settings → Privacy & Security → Demo Mode. While it is on your real data is not loaded — it is not gone, it simply isn't shown — and it comes straight back when you exit.

If the demo is OFF and you still see sample figures, that is different: sample data was actually written to your database at some point. Settings → Data & Backup → Remove Sample Data takes it out without touching anything you entered yourself.

t: My Watch shows different numbers than my phone
b:
The Watch is a thin client — it shows what the phone last sent it. If the phone hasn't been opened since the numbers moved, the Watch is showing the last thing it was told, correctly.

Open the app on the phone with the Watch nearby and give it a few seconds. If a complication is still behind, the watch face refreshes on its own schedule — opening the Watch app forces it.

t: I can't send a support message
b:
Two things gate that button, and both say so on screen now:

• A few characters are needed before it turns on — the line under the button counts down how many.
• The Send button sits below the keyboard on a long sheet. There is a Send in the row above the keyboard, so you never have to go looking for it.

If it says you are not signed into iCloud, the app opens Mail instead and nothing leaves until you hit send there. If sending fails outright, the exact reason is printed under the button — that message is the most useful thing you can pass on.

t: A big import is taking forever, or seems stuck
b:
A file with tens of thousands of rows genuinely takes a while, and the review step is deliberately not skipped — an import that writes first and asks later is how a ledger gets ruined.

Leave the app in the foreground while it works; iOS suspends background work and a suspended import looks exactly like a stuck one.

If it truly stops, close and reopen the app: nothing is written until you confirm the review, so you lose the parse and not your data. Then try a smaller date range — most exports let you pick one.

t: Text in a box is invisible, or I can't see what I'm typing
b:
This was a real bug in dark mode on the Report a Problem and Help search boxes, and it is fixed — update to the current version.

If you see it anywhere else, that is worth telling us about, with the screen name and whether you are in light or dark mode. It is the kind of fault that is invisible to whoever built the screen and obvious to whoever is using it.

t: A transfer between my accounts shows as spending
b:
Record it as a TRANSFER rather than as an expense with a matching income — then it moves the balances and stays out of income and spending, which is what you want. Otherwise the same money is counted twice, once each way.

An imported file often can't tell the difference. Edit the row and set it to a transfer; if the same pair comes in every month, a Rule will handle it from then on.

t: My budget looks broken the month I bought something big
b:
A wedding, a ring, a car or a new roof is not a monthly category, and forcing it into one makes twelve months look wrong to describe one purchase.

Add it as a one-time expense instead. It sits in the annual plan and deliberately stays out of every monthly budget, so the month it lands in still reads honestly.

t: Older shared transactions all say “Joint”
b:
They predate the app recording WHO added a row, so there is genuinely no name attached to them — “Joint” is the old default, not a mistake made about a specific person.

Everything added since is attributed to whoever entered it, and the feed, the split bar and the Mine / Theirs / Joint filter all read that. The old rows stay as they are rather than being guessed at.

t: I clicked a row and nothing happened
b:
On a Mac a single click SELECTS a row and a double-click OPENS it. That is the platform's rule rather than this app's, and it is the opposite of the phone, where one tap does both.

So: double-click a transaction to edit it, an account to open it, a merchant to see what is behind its total. Right-click gives you the same actions as a menu — and on the Mac that menu is also where the swipe actions from the iPhone live, because there is nothing to swipe.

If a double-click still does nothing on a row you expect to open, that is worth telling us about; say which screen.

t: A button on my Mac is black, or I can't read a control
b:
Update to the current version — this was a real bug and it is fixed.

Forty-two buttons across the Mac app drew as a black slab with a black label. They still worked; you just had to guess what they said. A switch had the same problem in reverse at night. Both were one wrong color token, and both are gone.

If you see anything unreadable on the current version, a screenshot is the single most useful thing you can send — Support → Report a problem takes one.

t: Set up your first budget
b: Pick categories and monthly limits in a couple minutes. Open the Budget tab. Add categories for your regular spending (rent, groceries, dining…). Set a monthly limit on each — round numbers are fine to start. As transactions come in, the rings fill so you see what's left.

t: Track your net worth
b: Add accounts and assets to see the full picture. Open Net Worth → Accounts. Add each account (cash, cards, loans, property, investments). Enter current balances — the Accounts view flags stale ones later. Watch the Overview trend chart build your net-worth history.

t: Import accounts & transactions
b: Bring in a statement from a photo or CSV. Open the Import tab. Choose a photo of a statement or a CSV file. Review the auto-classified rows — fix any category or type. Approve to save. Nothing imports until you say so.

t: Build a retirement plan
b: Model your path to financial independence. Open the Retirement tab → Setup. Enter income, savings, accounts, and a target retirement age. Switch to Analysis to stress-test with Monte Carlo & history. Use Report to export an investor-grade PDF.

t: Set a savings goal
b: Give every dollar a job with a target and deadline. Open the Goals tab. Create a goal (emergency fund, house, trip…). Set a target amount and optional date. Fund it over time and track progress at a glance.

t: Find your subscriptions
b: Auto-detected from your history — no manual entry. Open the Subscriptions tab. Review recurring charges detected from your transactions. Watch for the price-hike badges. Click Track to turn any into a bill that feeds your Budget & Forecast.

t: Learn the concepts
b: Guides, playbooks, paths, and a money glossary. Open the Learn tab. Start with a guided Path, or browse Guides & Playbooks. Search the glossary for any term you hit. Click the in-app links to act on what you just learned.

t: See your cash flow ahead
b: Know if you'll make it to payday — before it's a problem. Add your recurring bills and income (Transactions ▸ Recurring). Open Forecast. Read your lowest projected balance and safe-to-spend. Switch to the Calendar view to see each day's bills and income.

t: Check your financial health
b: One score, five pillars, and what to fix first. Open Financial Health. See your 0–100 score and letter grade. Read the 'Do this next' list of your weakest pillars. Click into the linked screen to act on each one.

t: Balance your investments
b: Set a target mix and see the exact moves to rebalance. Open Allocation. Set your target percentages per asset class. Review the drift and the buy/sell amounts to rebalance. Override any holding's auto-classification if needed.
